ideas.title: Climb anything: a grab that can slip
ideas.critique: This is the same project as last round's hang, now with the slip as the shot. That answers the main risk (a grab that looks scripted), but only if the slip comes out of the cone test with Lumi's real momentum and is not a coin flip per material tag. Load carried through friction contacts that can really fail is something the island has never done, and two takes on one wall, side by side, show cause and effect that you can read.

ideas.title: A boomerang that comes back
ideas.nearest: Skipping stones, a take that misses
same_form: Skipping stones, a take that misses
ideas.critique: It is still one thrown object filmed in flight, the island's most worn form, and the last two attempts at it missed on camera. A path that only comes back through blade-element lift and gyroscopic precession is real aerodynamics the island lacks, and a throw you learn by feel, ending in a catch, is a goal people repeat. The danger is a small object against the sky that the film loses.

ideas.title: Tippe tops on the cottage table
ideas.critique: A tippe top that inverts purely from sliding friction is the kind of counter-intuitive rigid-body result people clip, and it can't be faked convincingly: either the integrator handles spin, friction and contact properly or the top just falls over. The duel is thin as a game (spin and wait), and the whole thing hinges on contact friction staying stable at high spin rates.

ideas.title: Sailing on the real sea
ideas.critique: This is last round's sailing idea reworded, with the same strengths: sailing is a skill you get better at, and tacking toward a goal upwind gives it a goal. Buoyancy per corner on the real wave surface is a step toward it really floating, but four sample points is still the plain version, and an on-deck film of a sail and a horizon is the expected shot.

ideas.title: A hot air balloon that steers by height
ideas.critique: Steering only by finding wind layers is a clever control scheme, and a burner glowing in the envelope at dawn suits the path tracer. But the physics is an ODE for one temperature plus an invented wind profile, so it is mostly a parameterised drift, and its slow pace and long lag make for a calm toy more than a game you keep coming back to.
